L4-01.why: Elimination on the three alternates: C 'were' is a plural verb where the shape 'The trouble with the wheel ___ that it would' demands singular; D 'being that' is never correct on the ACT; B inserts a comma between subject and verb. Whatever No Change says, the three named alternates are each independently defective, so the untouched original is the residue.

L4-02.why: Punctuation-before-appositive set: colon / period / 'being' / original. D is out ('being' is always wrong). C makes 'A neighborhood tool library...' a likely fragment. That leaves the colon against the original, and the fact that the item bothers to offer a colon suggests the original is a weaker mark (semicolon or comma) before an explanatory appositive. Genuinely a coin flip between A and B; I took the colon.

L4-03.why: Yes/No rhetoric item, 2-2 split, so the split gives nothing. Picked on the rule that the key names BOTH halves of whatever compound goal the stem stated: C is the only option citing a mechanism ('how meanders migrate') AND a time element ('the decades involved'), which is the shape of a two-part goal statement. B and D are the 'No' pair and both concede the essay does something else; A is a plausible-sounding wrong 'Yes'. Real guess.

L4-04.why: Irregular-verb set for sink. A 'had sunken' is nonstandard as a verb; B 'was sunk' swaps to passive (a meaning change, not a grammar fix); C bare 'sunk' as a simple past is the classic wrong form. That leaves No Change, which is probably either 'sank' or 'had sunk' - both correct. Elimination only; I cannot see the original.

L4-05.why: Pure tense-consistency item and tense consistency is decided entirely by the surrounding sentence, which I do not have. Three alternates are past / future / present-progressive, i.e. a symmetric spread with no defective member. Defaulted to No Change because none of the three can be ruled out on its own. This is a guess.

L4-06.why: Diction/wordiness set: C 'in a big way' is colloquial and vague, D 'with vigorous and energetic intensity' is triple-redundant. The remaining contest is the original against a concise, specific, vivid phrase; ACT keys that phrase and makes the original the vague or wordy one. Standard 'one precise option among a vague one and a padded one' read.

L4-07.why: Add-a-clause item. A, B, D are all additive continuations; C is the only one that names a cause and reframes the point ('not because they are reckless but because the street tells them they can'), which fits the thesis such a passage almost certainly has - street design shapes driver behavior. Caveat I am recording deliberately: the concede-then-qualify shape is a known DISTRACTOR family in this bank, so this pick may be exactly the trap.

L4-08.why: Paragraph-function item. C self-marks as a distractor with the absolute 'the ONE obstacle that podcasts finally removed'. B is syntactically contorted and attributes a concession. A and D are both contrast claims; D reads as the measured forward-reference (this paragraph pictures X, a later paragraph contrasts it), which is the usual key shape. Weak; A is live.

L4-09.why: Redundancy item, decidable without any context: B 'In 1795, during that year' and D 'At the time of the year 1795' are overtly redundant, and No Change is presumably a third redundant variant. 'In 1795' is the only clean version.

L4-10.why: Subject-verb agreement with a plural subject visible inside the underlined text: 'the rains' takes 'leave'. A 'is leaving' and C 'has left' are both singular; No Change is presumably 'leaves'. The plural noun is inside the option, so this is decidable option-only.

L4-11.why: Sentence-choice item. C 'The markers were the trouble' is vague and refers to something I cannot check. A, B, D all plausible. Picked B for concreteness plus internal causal content ('rotting faster than the town could replace them'), on the general habit that the key sentence carries specific detail that the paragraph can develop. Effectively a guess between B and D.

L4-12.why: Countable quantifier item. 'less scouts' is the count/mass error; 'fewer of scouts' and 'less of scouts' are both unidiomatic partitives. All three alternates are defective on their face, so No Change ('fewer scouts') is the residue. Decidable option-only.

L4-13.why: Redundancy again: B 'today, currently', C 'Today, at the present time' are explicit doublings, and No Change is presumably a third. 'Today Okafor teaches' is the only non-redundant option. Same mechanism as L4-09.

L4-14.why: Register/tone item: A 'pretty decent, I guess' is too colloquial and hedged for expository prose; C 'of a demonstrably superior quality' is inflated and wordy. ACT keys the plain concrete phrase between the two extremes, so 'sharp and clean'. Assumes No Change is the fourth defective variant, which I cannot see.

L4-15.why: Agreement/tense item where the subject is NOT inside the underlined text, so I cannot see number. Options spread present-perfect-plural / original / present-singular / present-progressive-plural. Guessed the singular present on the weak prior that items written around 'depends' usually test an intervening prepositional phrase that makes a singular subject look plural. Coin flip with A.
